sm: The host welcomes James Holland, whom he describes as a market analyst, to talk about politics, the economy and how the wars might affect it. Asked why Republicans lost in November, Holland says polling showed a significant number of Republican-side voters flipped to Democrats, and others moved to independents. He puts it at roughly twenty-five percent who flopped out of agitation and seventy-five percent who flipped. He says the war in Iran was a big factor, since the party ran on no new wars and America first. He calls it a conflict rather than a formal war, and argues voters paying high gas prices had no good justification offered for the cost.

The host says he sees the war as about twenty percent of the problem and the resulting economics, like high gas prices, as eighty percent. Holland agrees and says the Iran conflict was added to a pot already boiling from the Ukraine war, where he cites at least 450,000 Russian deaths and 250,000 to 350,000 Ukrainian deaths. He notes the Houthis blew up a major Saudi refinery pipeline once the Strait of Hormuz calmed, which could take years to recover. He quotes Vice President Vance's framing that stopping an Iranian nuclear weapon was either worth losing Congress or it was not. On domestic oil, he says U.S. refineries are at ninety-eight percent capacity, and new refining capacity is at least a ten-year project.

Holland says the country is about eight years behind on refining, and that allies like Brazil are less helpful after Lula's win. The host then gives his own view of the economy: he says COVID shutdowns and stimulus caused self-inflicted inflation, which he puts around seventeen or eighteen percent through 2024, far above official figures. He adds that Trump's tariffs added roughly another five percent, bringing it to about twenty-five to twenty-eight percent. He says he supports tariffs as a tool against Chinese slave labor, but says Trump's claim that America is making money is misleading since the government collects it while businesses that trade with Italy and Mexico suffer. Holland agrees that nobody has been honest about the inflation.

The host says nobody told voters honestly about the stimulus-driven inflation or the tariff pain. He says Trump keeps calling the economy great while he is barely making it month to month, and his local school levy will raise his mortgage payment by about two hundred dollars. Holland says the Iran war is just the last name in the credits, after an unfinished tariff war, and that allies like Britain and France lack the ships, planes and troops to help anyway. He says diesel price rises pushed everything up. He suspects the war priorities came from people in Trump's cabinet and from long-time Washington insiders like Lindsey Graham, who assured him there would be no electoral cost.

Holland says the Iran pivot was not characteristic of Trump and that he could have asked five people under thirty their view of Iran. The conversation turns to interest rates. Holland says the real inflation is far above the five or six percent often cited, which is why rates stay high. He says the odds of a December rate hike rose from under fifty percent in July to over ninety percent now, and that rates should rise by a quarter or half point several times next year. He worries young people will be thirty-five before they can afford a down payment. He also criticizes James Talarico's claim that taxing the one percent would raise one hundred seventy-four billion dollars, noting that is less than the roughly one hundred eighty-six billion dollars of interest paid on health care.

Holland says the one hundred seventy-six billion dollar figure would not cover the real costs, and that Trump deserves credit for starting the Doge cuts, which got overshadowed by other events. The talk moves to Nvidia, whose stock has dropped to around one hundred sixty dollars after executive resignations tied to affair allegations. Holland says either the AI bubble is about to burst or Nvidia is among the best buys in the world. He notes data center projects are being pushed off, but argues those will move to other counties rather than disappear. He says people are buying heavily because they expect two hundred ten dollars next year, though tech stocks and semiconductors keep dropping.

Holland says that if Nvidia reaches two hundred ten to two hundred twenty dollars next year, buying at one hundred sixty would be a great move. He thinks that is more likely than the whole AI and data center story being fake, though we probably do not need as many data centers as proposed. For 2027, with Democrats in the House and Senate, he expects a stalemate, with the most likely legislation involving health care, tech and perhaps consumer pricing. He hopes for solar tax credits, says EV credits are likely gone, and expects oil traders to be on edge over missiles. He expects health care premium increases to push inflation higher. The host says his family deductible runs six to eight thousand dollars. They close by wishing listeners a good Thanksgiving week.
